title: gRPC keepalive + goroutine scheduling postmortem
summary: Postmortem of recurring P99 tail latency spikes observed in streaming gRPC requests for short prompt workloads. Investigation focused on interaction between gRPC keepalive, Go scheduler wakeups, and application-level goroutine bursts during KV-cache warmup and small-chunk streaming.
symptoms: Around 2026-11-10 we started seeing intermittent P99 spikes (2.5x baseline) for streaming endpoints that serve short prompts (<128 tokens) under moderate concurrency (~50-200 concurrent streams). Spikes lasted 50-200ms and correlated with higher syscall and context-switch activity on proxy/sidecar hosts. No model OOMs or GPU stalls were observed.
environment: Prod-like dedicated cluster (dedicated tier): 8x A100 nodes behind envoy sidecars, go-serving runtime v1.14, gRPC-go v1.57, network: 25GbE, sidecar proxies: envoy 1.26. Tests reproduced on staging (same artifact versions) with 16 client machines generating sustained streaming load via our loadgen harness.
hypothesis: gRPC keepalive probes and short-lived streaming goroutines produce bursts of timers/epoll wakeups that interact poorly with Go's scheduler on busy cores. The resulting CPU scheduling jitter manifests as tail-latency in small-chunk streaming where per-chunk processing time is tiny and therefore scheduling overhead dominates.
experiment-setup: Load profile: 120 concurrent streams, each stream sends 3 short chunks (avg 120 bytes) to produce ~10k tokens/s aggregate. Two configurations tested: (A) default keepalive (ClientKeepalive Time=30s, Server enforcement disabled), (B) aggressive keepalive (1s) used by a misconfigured proxy testbed, (C) disabled keepalive via proxy pass-through. Measurement: pprof CPU samples (5s/10s runs), go trace, eBPF sched records, tcpdump to capture keepalive/HTTP/2 frames. Repeated runs for statistical significance (10 runs each).
measurements:
Key metrics (median across runs):
- Baseline (default keepalive): P50=18ms, P95=64ms, P99=140ms, CPU usage: 42% system+user on sidecar, goroutines: ~6500.
- Aggressive keepalive (1s): P50=20ms, P95=120ms, P99=380ms, CPU spikes +20% on core 3-5, syscalls/s increased by 3.1x, context switches increased 2.8x.
- Keepalive disabled: P50=17ms, P95=58ms, P99=120ms, CPU usage slightly reduced.
Additional observations: go trace showed repeated preemption/wakeup cycles pinned to small intervals matching keepalive interval. eBPF sched shows increased runnable->running transitions for the gRPC listener goroutine and per-request goroutines coincident with keepalive bursts.
profiling-notes: CPU pprof flamegraphs show top stacks: net/http2.(*serverConn).serveStreams -> h2Stream readLoop -> runtime.netpoll -> runtime.schedule. User-space time dominated by http2 read/decode and HPACK for headers for every keepalive ping/pong and occasional control frames. Traces show short-lived goroutines created per incoming frame that incur scheduler overhead. The timer wheel and runtime timers scanned frequently at keepalive frequency in aggressive config.
root-cause-analysis: A confluence of factors: (1) Aggressive keepalive settings from a subset of test proxies caused frequent control frames and timer events, (2) gRPC/google's http2 implementation creates work on per-frame delivery which produces transient goroutine activity, (3) Go scheduler's wakeup cost and syscall/epoll churn under high core utilization produced jitter that disproportionately affects tiny per-chunk latencies (the signal-to-noise ratio is low). Secondary contributor: sidecar CPU affinity had tight packing causing timer processing to contend with the serving goroutine.
mitigations-applied: Immediate: rolled back aggressive keepalive configs in test fleet and enforced a minimum keepalive_time of 15s on proxies. Tuned envoy to use tcp keepalive only on idle connections instead of active streaming. Adjusted sidecar CPU pinning to separate timer/IO cores from processing cores (affinity change). Result: P99 dropped back to ~130ms and spikes largely disappeared.
longer-term-recommendations:
1) Add defensive server-side guard: rate-limit processing of control frames and coalesce small timer events in the serving runtime.
2) Update our recommended proxy configuration in the docs: keepalive >= 15s for streaming endpoints; avoid proxy-inserted aggressive probes.
3) Add a lightweight connection health-check that avoids full HTTP/2 control frames for high-churn clients.
4) Investigate moving hpkt/HPACK decoding to a buffered worker to reduce per-frame goroutine churn.
5) Run experiments with go1.21/1.22 scheduler improvements and measure improvements.
6) Add automated regression tests in CI that replay keepalive/control-frame bursts and assert tail-latency bounds.
open-questions:
- Would using HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming for very small-payload workloads reduce scheduler churn? (initial microbench suggests yes for tiny chunks but worse at higher concurrency).
- Can we safely relax server-side timer granularity without affecting idle connection cleanup?
- Is there value in explicit connection pooling to reduce per-client control-frame noise?
next_steps:
1) Create RFC for proxy keepalive policy and land a doc change (owner: Marta).
2) Prototype buffered HPACK decode worker and benchmark (owner: Ethan).
3) Schedule an infra change for CPU affinity on sidecars in Dedicated (owner: Jonah).
4) Add a JMH-style replay harness in CI to simulate keepalive bursts (owner: Priya).
conclusion: Tail-latency spikes for small-chunk streaming were not a GPU or model issue but a networking+runtime interaction: frequent control frames and timer wakeups amplified by goroutine scheduling overhead. Operational fixes (keepalive policy, CPU pinning) mitigated the problem; engineering work (coalescing timers, buffered decode) can make the system more robust against noisy clients and aggressive proxies.
notes-to-self: Keep an eye on any config drifts from proxies managed by partner teams; add an alert rule for sudden Syscall/sec increases on sidecars. Save raw pprof and trace bundles under /tmp/prof-2026-11-15 for root-cause forensic purposes.
